Pretest

Learning Objectives
Review the relevant anatomy of the posterior tibial tendon.
Identify the stages of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
Review nonsurgical strategies to manage posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the most common cause of adult acquired flatfoot
deformity (AAFD), which recently was reclassified as progressive collapsing flatfoot deformity.1
Although overuse often is cited as the cause of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, the exact
etiology is unknown. The disease typically occurs in a watershed region just distal to the
medial malleolus. The watershed area is approximately 14 mm long and approximately 40 mm
proximal to the tendon insertion site.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The complexity of the pathologic process of progressive collapsing flatfoot deformity is
only partially understood. The medial longitudinal arch of the foot is dynamically
supported by the posterior tibial tendon, whereas static restraints include the spring,
talocalcaneal, cervical, and interosseus, as well as the superficial and deep deltoid
ligaments.2 The posterior tibial tendon inserts at the navicular tuberosity and several
other tarsal/metatarsal structures to plantarflex and invert the foot. This foot inversion
causes locking of the transverse tarsal joints to allow for foot stability during push-off.
The deltoid and spring ligament act as a functional unit and as the primary static
stabilizer of the medial arch. The posterior tibial tendon acts as a secondary stabilizer of
the medial arch.
If this dynamic support of the posterior tibial tendon and the deltoid-spring ligament
complex fails, the transverse tarsal joints become unstable, allowing the peroneus brevis
to act unopposed and causing forefoot abduction. The medial column can collapse at
any or all the following joints: talonavicular, naviculocuneiform, and first tarsometatarsal
joints. As the forefoot abducts and the tarsal joints destabilize, the force of the Achilles
tendon is displaced, contributing to hindfoot valgus and subtalar instability. Persistent
hindfoot valgus eventually causes compensatory forefoot varus/supination (first ray
elevation), which is supple at first but becomes fixed as pathology progresses.

As the midfoot strains, the static stabilizers attenuate. If the spring ligament fails, loss of
peritalar stability occurs, causing the talus to assume a more medial and plantarflexed
position relative to the navicular. As pathology progresses, the deltoid ligament
attenuates, leading to increased tibiotalar valgus angulation and disturbances in talar
axial rotation.
Epidemiology
Females in their fifties
Obesity
Inflammatory arthropathy
Other reported risk factors include hypertension and diabetes mellitus
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The tibialis posterior muscle is innervated by the posterior tibial nerve (L4-L5) and originates
from the posterior fibula, tibia, and interosseous membrane.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The tendon travels distally, running posterior to the medial malleolus before dividing
into three limbs. The anterior limb inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular and the
first cuneiform.
The middle limb inserts into the second and third cuneiforms, the cuboid, and the
second through fifth metatarsals. The posterior limb inserts on the sustentaculum tali
anteriorly.
The tibialis posterior tendon lies in an axis posterior to the ankle joint and medial to the
axis of the subtalar joint (it is the tendon insertion point farthest from the fulcrum of the
subtalar joint). It acts as an invertor of the hindfoot and adducts and supinates the
forefoot during the stance phase of gait. It also acts as a secondary plantar flexor of the
ankle.

The tibialis posterior tendon elevates the medial longitudinal arch and locks the
transverse tarsal joints, creating a rigid lever arm during the terminal stance phase of
gait. The major antagonist to the tibialis posterior tendon is the peroneus brevis tendon,
which serves to evert the hindfoot. The normal excursion of the tendon is approximately
2 cm.



flexibility of the presenting deformity according to the Johnson and Strom 1989

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Classic findings of prolonged involvement include (Figure 1):
Collapse of the medial longitudinal arch
Hindfoot valgus
Forefoot abduction and varus (the too many toes sign)
Elevated first ray (forefoot supination)
Figure 1 Anterior (A) and posterior (B) photographs of the feet and ankles of a patient with long-
standing tibialis posterior tendon insufficiency. Note the classic physical findings: a collapsed
medial longitudinal arch, hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction, and varus (the too many toes sign).
(Reproduced from Lee S, Lin J: Tendon disorders of the foot and ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1182-1196.)

Patient History and Physical Examination
Assess hindfoot alignment
Assess forefoot abduction
Evaluate for Achilles tendon/gastrocnemius contracture
Rigid deformity

Patient History and Physical Examination
The physical examination begins by observing the patient from the front, side, and back
with the patient standing. The overall general alignment of the limb and approximate leg
lengths should be noted. With the patient’s back toward the examiner, hindfoot
alignment is noted. At the same time, the examiner can evaluate for the too many toes
sign. The too many toes sign is positive if the examiner observes the patient from behind
and more toes are observed lateral to the tibia on the affected foot compared with the
contralateral foot. The posterior tibial edema sign is described as objective evidence of
posterior tibialis tendon dysfunction if pitting edema is observed along the course of the
posterior tibialis tendon posterior to the medial malleolus.
A single-limb heel raise is a crucial test for evaluating the posterior tibialis tendon. The
patient is asked to stand on the toes of the affected limb. The patient may use the wall
for balance. In patients who can perform a single-leg heel raise, the posterior tibialis
tendon likely is intact, whereas inability to perform a single-leg heel raise suggests
posterior tibialis tendon pathology. Earlier stages are associated with various physical
examination findings. Typically, the pain begins medially along the posterior tibial
tendon and then progresses laterally with the development of lateral impingement. In
the later stages, the hindfoot and/or forefoot deformity may become fixed. The patient
also loses the ability to perform a single-limb heel rise because of two reasons:
Inability to lock the transverse tarsal joints to create a rigid lever arm
Valgus displacement of the calcaneus that results in a weakened Achilles tendon
moment arm

The examiner also must assess for an Achilles tendon or gastrocnemius contracture. The
Silverskiöld test is used to differentiate a tight gastrocnemius from a tight Achilles
tendon. The test is performed by comparing dorsiflexion of the ankle with the patient’s
knee extended and dorsiflexion of the ankle with the patient’s knee flexed to 90°.
Because the gastrocnemius crosses the knee and ankle joints, the muscle can be
effectively lengthened with knee flexion. Therefore, an increase in ankle dorsiflexion with
the knee flexed localizes the contracture to the gastrocnemius. No change in ankle
dorsiflexion in the extended and flexed knee localizes the contracture to the Achilles
tendon.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing radiographs of the foot and ankle should be obtained in all patients with
posterior tibial tendon dysfunction. Radiographs typically reveal:
Loss of the Meary (talar–first metatarsal) angle
Loss of calcaneal pitch
Variable degrees of peritalar subluxation
Talonavicular coverage angle (Figure 2)

Figure 2 Weight-bearing radiographs of a foot and ankle with tibialis posterior tendon
dysfunction. A, AP radiograph demonstrates peritalar subluxation. Note the loss of the expected
parallel lines of the talonavicular coverage angle. Also note the forefoot abduction and the
associated degenerative changes of the adjacent metatarsal-cuneiform and cuneiform-navicular
joints (arrows). B, Lateral radiograph demonstrates loss of parallelism between the talus and the
first metatarsal (X) and almost completely absent calcaneal pitch (Y). (Reproduced from Lee S, Lin
J: Tendon disorders of the foot and ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1182-1196.)

Radiography
Standing AP and lateral radiographs of the foot and ankle, including a hindfoot
alignment view, are critical. Radiographs help refine staging and surgical correction.
Most importantly, radiographs help determine the apex of deformity. Any medial column
collapse observed on lateral radiographs indicates insufficiency of the pertaining
ligaments of that joint. On lateral radiographs, medial column position and alignment
are assessed via the talo-first metatarsal or the Meary angle. The angle is subtended by
the longitudinal axis of the talus and the first metatarsal. A measurement of 15° to 30° is
considered moderate progressive collapsing flatfoot deformity. Pes planus deformity is
considered severe if the Meary angle is greater than 30°.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001014
9/23

On lateral radiographs, plantar gapping or arthritis at the first tarsometatarsal joint
indicates medial column instability. Talonavicular and naviculocuneiform arthritis or
sagging also should be noted because any collapse through these joints represents
insufficiency of the ligaments associated with stabilizing the joint. Overlap of the talus
and calcaneus also should be noted. Medial arch sag also can be quantified via the
medial arch sag angle. The medial arch sag angle is the angle created by a line drawn
along the articular surface of the navicular and a line drawn parallel to the first
tarsometatarsal joint.
On AP radiographs, the talonavicular coverage angle should be measured because it
indicates the severity of forefoot abduction and dorsolateral peritalar subluxation. The
talar incongruency angle is another reliable and validated radiographic measurement
used to assess severity of forefoot abduction. As medial column support fails, the
talonavicular joint abducts and the subtalar joint everts and pronates. On normal
radiographs, the calcaneocuboid and talonavicular joints are parallel and even. If the
lateral column is short, the talonavicular joint will appear to be 3 to 5 mm distal to the
calcaneocuboid joints.
Stage IIa AAFD involves deformity with less severe abduction through the midfoot (less
than 30% talar head uncoverage observed on AP radiographs (Figure 3). In Stage IIb,
patients generally have more deformity clinically, with greater than 30% talar head
uncoverage observed on standing AP radiographs. As the deformity through the
talonavicular joint becomes more severe, greater foot abduction occurs at that joint. This
can be observed if standing radiographs demonstrate uncoverage of the medial talar
head (Figure 4). Stage III AAFD involves fixed deformity (no passive inversion or eversion;
Figure 5).

Computed Tomography
Primarily used to detect hindfoot coalition or arthritis

Computed Tomography
Weight-bearing CT scans have been used to evaluate for various deformities, subtalar
instability (Figure 7), and subfibular impingement3 (Figure 8).
Figure 7 Weight-bearing CT scans show the difference in subtalar joint alignment
between the foot of a patient with adult acquired flatfoot deformity (A) and the foot of a
patient with normal hindfoot alignment (B). At 50% of the AP length of the posterior
facet, the patient with adult acquired flatfoot deformity has notable valgus alignment of
the subtalar joint, which is demonstrated by the inferior facet of the talus and the
horizontal white line. In the patient with hallux valgus at 50% of the AP length of the
posterior facet, slight varus alignment of the subtalar joint is observed (black line).

Measurements of joint alignment and angles have been shown to be more accurate on
cone-beam weight-bearing CT scans than on conventional radiographs and non–weight-
bearing CT scans. This may offer clinical advantages for planning deformity correction
preoperatively compared with conventional modalities.
Radiation exposure in cone-beam weight-bearing CT scanners has been estimated to be
approximately 10% to 66% less than that of conventional multidetector CT scanners. For
centers that do not have access to a weight-bearing CT scanner, a traditional CT scanner
with an axial loading device that is able to produce greater than 70% of a patient’s body

Ultrasonography has played an increasing role in evaluating pathology in the tibialis posterior
tendon.

This modality usually is office-based and less costly than MRI. It also is a dynamic test and
allows for evaluation of the tendon without risk of the magic angle effect, creating distortion in
interpretation of tendon pathology.
Nonsurgical Management
Treatment Goals
The goals of nonsurgical management are to improve function, decrease pain, protect the
tendon, and prevent deformity progression. In general, management is based on disease
stage.

Treatment Goals
In stage I disease, the posterior tibial tendon is at particular risk for injury and
progression to later disease stages. The patient usually is exquisitely tender; therefore,
management should focus on rest and decreasing motion/inflammation. NSAIDs may be
prescribed for 2 to 4 weeks. Usually, a controlled ankle motion boot also is prescribed
for 4 to 6 weeks. At the same time, daily NSAID therapy often is initiated. A corticosteroid
injection is never indicated. Thereafter, physical therapy, focusing on inversion and
plantar flexion strengthening and gastrocnemius stretching, often is initiated.
In stage II disease, the posterior tibial tendon is dysfunctional (a length deficit is present
in the tendon). Successful outcomes have been reported with the use of a controlled
ankle motion boot for 4 to 6 weeks followed by physical therapy and the use of semirigid
orthoses. Medial hindfoot posting can be used to correct heel valgus (Figure 10).

Figure 10 Lateral (A), anterior (B), dorsal (C), and medial (D) view clinical photographs
show a custom insert with semirigid longitudinal arch support and medial posting.
(Courtesy of Christopher Edward Gross, MD, FAAOS, Charleston, SC.)
In stage III and stage IV disease, rigid deformities generally are managed with the use of
soft, accommodative shoe orthoses. Patients with more advanced or painful deformity
may respond to immobilization with ankle-foot orthoses (Figure 11; Videos 1 and 2).
Attempting to correct the alignment of rigid deformities may result in pain and skin
breakdown. Corticosteroid injections should never be administered about the posterior
tibial tendon because of the risk for tendon rupture; however, intra-articular injections
may be useful in the management of associated hindfoot arthritis.
